source.title: What to Wear as a Wedding Guest
source.author: Gentleman's Gazette

tips.text: As a wedding guest, don't upstage the couple: stick to sober colours and simple patterns unless the invitation encourages more.
tips.why: Attention belongs to the couple and the wedding party.

tips.text: Avoid an all-black suit, shirt and tie combination at a wedding.
tips.why: The monochrome look is dated and grabs attention.

tips.text: Leave top hats, ascots, gloves and showy boutonnieres to the wedding party unless you're asked to wear them.
tips.why: Those pieces signal a special role in the ceremony.

tips.text: Follow the wedding invitation's dress code exactly, neither under- nor overdressing.
tips.why: Ignoring it is rude, and dressing above it can upstage the groom.

tips.text: Start planning a wedding-guest outfit at least a month before the date.
tips.why: It leaves time to find pieces and get alterations done.

tips.text: Unless the invitation allows it, don't wear sandals, flip-flops, shorts, T-shirts, hoodies, trainers or casual jeans to a wedding.
tips.why: They are far too casual for the occasion.

tips.text: If ceremony and reception have different dress codes and there's no time to change, dress for the more formal one.
tips.why: Being slightly overdressed at the party beats being underdressed at the ceremony.

tips.text: Daytime, warm-weather and outdoor weddings allow lighter, more relaxed clothes; weddings in places of worship call for more formality.
tips.why: Time, season and venue shift how formal the day is.

tips.text: Navy and charcoal suits are the most versatile wedding-guest choices, in lighter or heavier wool depending on the season.
tips.why: Sober dark colours fit almost any dress code.

tips.text: At a wedding, wear dark brown oxfords or derbies by day and black ones in the evening.
tips.why: Black reads more formal and suits evening events.

tips.text: A necktie suits most wedding dress codes; save bow ties for formal evening events.
tips.why: A bow tie with a day suit can look whimsical.

tips.text: For a cocktail-attire wedding, wear a dark grey or navy suit with a white or light blue shirt, or dark brown for an outdoor daytime event.
tips.why: Dark suits meet the code without straying into black tie.

tips.text: For black tie optional, a plain dark grey or dark blue suit with a white shirt and black plain-toe oxfords is the right alternative to a tuxedo.
tips.why: It matches the formality without a dinner suit.

tips.text: A tuxedo should be black or midnight blue, not a brighter blue.
tips.why: Other colours break the black-tie code.

tips.text: Add personality with a pocket square and a small boutonniere in a harmonising colour, balanced so neither overpowers the other.
tips.why: Small accents show care without stealing attention.

tips.text: The more formal the wedding, the more restrained your accessories should be.
tips.why: Formal dress codes leave less room for flourishes.

tips.text: For outdoor summer weddings, linen or seersucker suits are good choices.
tips.why: They keep you cool and suit warm daytime settings.

tips.text: Avoid white clothing that could compete with the bride.
tips.why: White is traditionally reserved for her.

outfits.outfit: jacket navy smart +suit, shirt white smart, trousers navy smart +suit, dress-shoes black formal +oxford
outfits.why: A navy suit, white shirt and black oxfords meets an evening cocktail-attire wedding.

outfits.outfit: jacket charcoal formal +suit, shirt white formal, trousers charcoal formal +suit, dress-shoes black formal +oxford +plain-toe
outfits.why: A solid dark grey suit with a white shirt and black plain-toe oxfords is the right answer to black tie optional.

outfits.outfit: jacket black smart +suit, shirt black smart, trousers black smart +suit, tie black smart
outfits.why: Head-to-toe black suit, shirt and tie is dated and draws attention at a wedding.
